section.heading: 2.4. Limits
Introduction to Calculus
section.paragraph: Historically, the development of calculus by Isaac Newton (1642–1727) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) resulted from the investigation of the following problems:

list.item: Finding the tangent line to a curve at a given point on the curve (Figure 26a)
Finding the area of a planar region bounded by an arbitrary curve (Figure 26b)

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b, plot a curve with a tangent line and a planar region on x y coordinate respectively. In graph a, the curve enter the second quadrant from the bottom left of the viewing window, slopes upward to the right, cuts the vertical axis, further arch down slightly and then plateaus at a point P. Thereafter the curve dips, slopes upward to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. A slanting tangent passes through the point P. A text below the graph reads, what is the slope of the tangent line T at point P? In graph b, a bean seed shaped planar region is plotted in the first quadrant, which is labeled R. A text below the graph reads, what is the area of the region R?

section.paragraph: The tangent-line problem might appear to be unrelated to any practical applications of mathematics, but as you will see later, the problem of finding the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another is mathematically equivalent to the geometric problem of finding the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a given point on the curve. It is precisely the discovery of the relationship between these two problems that spurred the development of calculus in the seventeenth century and made it such an indispensable tool for solving practical problems. The following are a few examples of such problems:

list.item: Finding the velocity of an object
Finding the rate of change of a bacteria population with respect to time
Finding the rate of change of a company’s profit with respect to time
Finding the rate of change of a travel agency’s revenue with respect to the agency’s expenditure for advertising

section.paragraph: The study of the tangent-line problem led to the creation of differential calculus, which relies on the concept of the derivative of a function. The study of the area problem led to the creation of integral calculus, which relies on the concept of the antiderivative, or integral, of a function. (The derivative of a function and the integral of a function are intimately related, as you will see in Section 6.4.) Both the derivative of a function and the integral of a function are defined in terms of a more fundamental concept: the limit, our next topic.

section.paragraph: Suppose we want to find the velocity of the maglev at $$t = 2$$ . This is just the velocity of the maglev as shown on its speedometer at that precise instant of time. Offhand, calculating this quantity using only Equation (3) appears to be an impossible task; but consider what quantities we can compute using this relationship. Obviously, we can compute the position of the maglev at any time $$t$$ as we did earlier for some selected values of $$t$$ . Using these values, we can then compute the average velocity of the maglev over an interval of time. For example, the average velocity of the train over the time interval $$\lbrack 2,4\rbrack$$ is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{ \text{Distance covered} }{ \text{Time elapsed} } = \frac{f(4) - f(2)}{4 - 2}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{ \text{Distance covered} }{ \text{Time elapsed} }} = \frac{4{(4^{2})} - 4{(2^{2})}}{2}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{ \text{Distance covered} }{ \text{Time elapsed} }} = \frac{64 - 16}{2} = 24} \end{array}$$
or $$24{feet} \slash {second}\left( {ft} \slash \sec \right)$$ .
Although this is not quite the velocity of the maglev at $$t = 2$$ , it does provide us with an approximation of its velocity at that time.

Can we do better? Intuitively, the smaller the time interval we pick (with $$t = 2$$ as the left endpoint), the better the average velocity over that time interval will approximate the actual velocity of the maglev at $$t = 2$$ .*
Actually, any interval containing $$t = 2$$ will do.
Now, let’s describe this process in general terms. Let $$t > 2$$ . Then, the average velocity of the maglev over the time interval $$\lbrack 2,t\rbrack$$ is given by

By choosing the values of $$t$$ closer and closer to $$2$$ , we obtain a sequence of numbers that give the average velocities of the maglev over smaller and smaller time intervals. As we observed earlier, this sequence of numbers should approach the instantaneous velocity of the train at $$t = 2$$ .
Let’s try some sample calculations. Using Equation (4) and taking the sequence $$t = 2.5,2.1,2.01,2.001$$ , and $$2.0001$$ , which approaches $$2$$ , we find:

list.item: The average velocity over $$\lbrack 2,2.5\rbrack$$ is $$\frac{4{({2.5^{2} - 4})}}{2.5 - 2} = 18$$ , or $$18{feet} \slash {second}$$ .
The average velocity over $$\lbrack 2,2.1\rbrack$$ is $$\frac{4{({2.1^{2} - 4})}}{2.1 - 2} = 16.4$$ , or $$16.4{feet} \slash {second}$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe that $$g(t)$$ approaches the number $$16$$ as $$t$$ approaches $$2$$ —this time from the left-hand side. In other words, as $$t$$ approaches $$2$$ from either side of $$2$$ , $$g(t)$$ approaches $$16$$ . In this situation, we say that the limit of $$g(t)$$ as $$t$$ approaches $$2$$ is $$16$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2}g(t) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({t^{2} - 4})}}{t - 2} = 16$$

section.paragraph: Observe that the point $$t = 2$$ is not in the domain of the function $$g$$ [for this reason, the point $$(2,16)$$ is missing from the graph of $$g$$ ]. This, however, is inconsequential because the value, if any, of $$g(t)$$ at $$t = 2$$ plays no role in computing the limit.
This example leads to the following informal definition.

note.title: Limit of a Function
note.heading: Limit of a Function
note.paragraph: The function $$f$$ has the limit $$L$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
if the value of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to the number $$L$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to (but not equal to) $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: Until now, we have relied on knowing the actual values of a function or the graph of a function near $$x = a$$ to help us evaluate the limit of the function $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ . The following properties of limits, which we list without proof, enable us to evaluate limits of functions algebraically.

note.title: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits
note.heading: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits
note.paragraph: Suppose
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = M$$
Then

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{r} = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}\rbrack}^{r} = L^{r} {r, \text{a positive constant} }$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}cf(x) = c\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = cL {c, \text{a real number} }$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) \pm g(x)} \right\rbrack = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) \pm \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = L \pm M$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}\rbrack}{\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)}\rbrack} = LM$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)} = \frac{L}{M} { \text{Provided that} M \neq 0}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Use Theorem 1 to evaluate the following limits.

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1}$$

example.heading: Solution

list.item: $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3} = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x}\rbrack}^{3} { \text{Property} 1}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3}} = 2^{3} = 8 {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x = 2}} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2} = 5{\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}x^{3 \slash 2}}\rbrack} { \text{Property} 2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}5x^{3 \slash 2}} = 5(4)^{3 \slash 2} = 40 { \text{Property} 1}} \end{array}$$

$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}5x^{4} - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2 { \text{Property} 3}$$ To evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2$$ , observe that the constant function $$g(x) = 2$$ has value $$2$$ for all values of $$x$$ . Therefore, $$g(x)$$ must approach the limit $$2$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$1$$ (or any other point for that matter!). Therefore, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} = 5(1)^{4} - 2 = 3$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} = 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} { \text{Property} 2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} { \text{Property} 4}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2(3)^{3}\sqrt{3^{2} + 7} {{Properties}1{and}3}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2(27)\sqrt{16} = 216} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {2x^{2} + 1} \right)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {x + 1} \right)} { \text{Property} 5}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1}} = \frac{2(2)^{2} + 1}{2 + 1} = \frac{9}{3} = 3} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Indeterminate Forms
section.paragraph: Let’s emphasize once again that Property $$5$$ of limits is valid only when the limit of the function that appears in the denominator is not equal to zero at the number in question.

If the numerator has a limit different from zero and the denominator has a limit equal to zero, then the limit of the quotient does not exist at the number in question. This is the case with the function $$g(x) = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ in Example 3b. Here, as $$x$$ approaches zero, the numerator approaches $$1$$ but the denominator approaches zero, so the quotient becomes arbitrarily large. Thus, as was observed earlier, the limit does not exist.
Next, consider
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2}$$

which we evaluated earlier by looking at the values of the function for $$x$$ near $$x = 2$$ . If we attempt to evaluate this expression by applying Property $$5$$ of limits, we see that both the numerator and denominator of the function

approach zero as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ ; that is, we obtain an expression of the form $$0 \slash 0$$ . In this event, we say that the limit of the quotient $$f(x) \slash g(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ has the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ .

We need to evaluate limits of this type when we discuss the derivative of a function, a fundamental concept in the study of calculus. As the name suggests, the meaningless expression $$0 \slash 0$$ does not provide us with a solution to our problem. One strategy that can be used to solve this type of problem follows.

list.item: Replace the given function with an appropriate one that takes on the same values as the original function everywhere except at $$x = a$$ .
Evaluate the limit of this function as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ .

section.heading: Limits at Infinity
section.paragraph: Up to now, we have studied the limit of a function as $$x$$ approaches a (finite) number $$a$$ . There are occasions, however, when we want to know whether $$f(x)$$ approaches a unique number as $$x$$ increases without bound. Consider, for example, the function $$P$$ , giving the number of fruit flies (Drosophila) in a container under controlled laboratory conditions, as a function of a time $$t$$ . The graph of $$P$$ is shown in Figure 33. You can see from the graph of $$P$$ that as $$t$$ increases without bound (gets larger and larger), $$P(t)$$ approaches the number $$400$$ . This number, called the carrying capacity of the environment, is determined by the amount of living space and food available, as well as other environmental factors.

section.paragraph: In the general case, the following definition for a limit of a function at infinity is applicable.

note.source_type: Limit of a Function at Infinity
note.title: Limit of a Function at Infinity
note.heading: Limit of a Function at Infinity
note.paragraph: The function $$f$$ has the limit $$L$$ as $$x$$ increases without bound (or as $$x$$ approaches infinity), written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$
if $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by taking $$x$$ large enough.
Similarly, the function $$f$$ has the limit $$M$$ as $$x$$ decreases without bound (or as $$x$$ approaches negative infinity), written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = M$$
if $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$M$$ by taking $$x$$ to be negative and sufficiently large in absolute value.

section.paragraph: All the properties of limits listed in Theorem 1 are valid when $$a$$ is replaced by $$\infty$$ or $$- \infty$$ . In addition, we have the following property for the limit at infinity.

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: For all $$n > 0$$ ,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{n}} = 0$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{n}} = 0$$
provided that $$\frac{1}{x^{n}}$$ is defined.

section.paragraph: We often use the following technique to evaluate the limit at infinity of a rational function: Divide the numerator and denominator of the expression by $$x^{n}$$ , where $$n$$ is the highest power present in the denominator of the expression.

example.heading: Example 8
Solution
example.paragraph: Since the limits of both the numerator and the denominator do not exist as $$x$$ approaches infinity, the property pertaining to the limit of a quotient (Property 5) is not applicable. Let’s divide the numerator and denominator of the rational expression by $$x^{3}$$ , obtaining

example.heading: Example 9
Solution
example.paragraph: Again, we see that Property 5 is not applicable. Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain

list.item: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x)$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x)$$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator of the rational expression by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x - 3 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{4}{x^{2}}}$$ Since the numerator becomes arbitrarily large, whereas the denominator approaches $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches infinity, we see that the quotient $$f(x)$$ gets larger and larger as $$x$$ approaches infinity. In other words, the limit does not exist. In this case, we indicate this by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \infty$$

Once again, dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x - 3 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{4}{x^{2}}}$$ In this case, the numerator becomes arbitrarily large in magnitude but negative in sign, whereas the denominator approaches $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches negative infinity. Therefore, the quotient $$f(x)$$ decreases without bound, and the limit does not exist. In this case, we indicate this by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = - \infty$$

section.paragraph: Example 11 gives an application of the concept of the limit of a function at infinity.

note.title: Applied Example 11. Average Cost Functions
note.heading: Applied Example 11. Average Cost Functions
note.paragraph: Custom Office makes a line of executive desks. It is estimated that the total cost of making $$x$$ Senior Executive Model desks is $$C(x) = 100x + 200,000$$ dollars per year, so the average cost of making $$x$$ desks is given by
$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{C}(x) = \frac{C(x)}{x}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{C}(x)} = \frac{100x + 200,000}{x} = 100 + \frac{200,000}{x}} \end{array}$$
dollars per desk. Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\overline{C}(x)$$ and interpret your results.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\overline{C}(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( 100 + \frac{200,000}{x} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\overline{C}(x)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}100 + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{200,000}{x} = 100} \end{array}$$

A sketch of the graph of the function $$\overline{C}(x)$$ appears in Figure 36. The result we obtained is fully expected if we consider its economic implications. Note that as the level of production increases, the fixed cost per desk produced, represented by the term $$(200,000 \slash x)$$ , drops steadily. The average cost should approach a constant unit cost of production— $$\$ 100$$ in this case.
